summary: Defines the binary attribute option for LDAP, which asks that attribute values be encoded with X.500 Basic Encoding Rules (BER) rather than the usual LDAP-specific encoding. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: A switch that says send this in raw machine form instead of the usual readable text.

questions: what is the ldap binary option
what does ldap binary attribute option do
when should i use ldap binary encoding
what is ber encoding in ldap
subtitle: A tag you add to an LDAP attribute name to say its values travel in raw BER form instead of the usual text form.

tldr.problem: Each LDAP attribute normally travels in a text-style, LDAP-specific encoding, but some kinds of values, such as certificates, are defined only in their binary BER form and need a way to be marked that way.
tldr.mechanism: The binary option is an attribute option string, "binary", added to an attribute description. It says the values are, or are requested to be, BER encoded.
tldr.outcome: The option was dropped from the revised LDAP specification, and this RFC brings it back for syntaxes that require it. Using it elsewhere is to be avoided.

today: RFC 4522 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains the definition of the LDAP binary option, which is meant for syntaxes such as certificates that require binary transfer.

sections.title: Why a Binary Option Exists
sections.content:
Every attribute in an LDAP directory has a syntax, which is its data type. The description of each syntax says how values are normally written when they cross the wire. The RFC calls that the LDAP-specific encoding.

RFC 4522 defines the binary option. When it appears in an attribute description in an LDAP operation, the attribute values or assertion values are, or are requested to be, encoded with the Basic Encoding Rules (BER) used by X.500 directories, instead of the usual LDAP-specific encoding.
sections.plainLanguage: Most things in the directory come written in a simple readable form. The binary option asks for the other, more machine-like form.

sections.title: History of the Option
sections.content:
The binary option was first defined in RFC 2251. The LDAP technical specification in RFC 4510 obsoleted the older one in RFC 3377, which included RFC 2251. The revised specification left the option out for a variety of reasons, including implementation inconsistencies. This RFC makes no attempt to resolve those inconsistencies.

What it does is reintroduce the option for attribute syntaxes that specifically require it, such as the certificate syntax in RFC 4523. It does not address using the option with syntaxes that do not require it, and says that such use is to be avoided unless a future specification covers it.
sections.plainLanguage: The sticker was thrown out once because people used it in different ways. Now it is back, but only for the few things that really need it.

sections.title: How the Binary Option Works
sections.content:
The option is written as the string binary in an attribute description. Like all attribute options it is case insensitive. Where it is present, the values MUST be BER encoded. Where it is absent, they use the LDAP-specific encoding of the attribute's syntax. In protocol terms, the contents octets of the AttributeValue or AssertionValue OCTET STRING are a complete BER encoding of the value.

It is not a tagging option, so it does not create an attribute subtype. An attribute description with binary refers to exactly the same attribute as one without it, and subtype relationships are not changed.

An attribute description SHALL be treated as unrecognized if it contains the option and the attribute's syntax has no associated ASN.1 type, or if BER encoding of that type is not supported. The option only affects transfer in the protocol. Servers store values in whatever format they choose.
sections.plainLanguage: Adding the word binary to a name does not make a new thing. It only says how to pack the same thing for the trip. How the server keeps it at home is its own business.

sections.title: Syntaxes That Require Binary Transfer
sections.content:
Some syntaxes are defined without any LDAP-specific encoding and must be sent in BER form. The RFC says these have a binary transfer requirement. Examples are the certificate, certificate list, certificate pair and supported algorithm syntaxes from RFC 4523.

These syntaxes also require that the exact BER encoding be preserved. The RFC stresses that this is a property of the syntaxes, not of the binary option. Without it, LDAP clients would need to re-encode values using the Distinguished Encoding Rules (DER).
sections.plainLanguage: A few things, like digital ID cards, only exist in the machine code form. For those, the exact bytes must arrive untouched.

sections.title: Search Requests and Results
sections.content:
A search request carries a list of requested attributes. That list MAY contain descriptions with the binary option, but MUST NOT contain two descriptions with the same attribute type and the same tagging options, even if only one has the option. The option implicitly applies to all subtypes of the requested attribute.

If an attribute has a binary transfer requirement and is returned, it SHALL come back in binary form, with the option in its description, whether or not the request included the option. For other attributes, the server SHOULD return the form that was asked for, and MAY omit an attribute if it does not support the requested encoding. A given value is returned at most once.

When the request list is empty or contains the special asterisk description, all user attributes are requested. Attributes with a binary transfer requirement are returned in binary form. Attributes without one that have an LDAP-specific encoding SHOULD NOT be returned in binary form. Those with neither may be returned in binary form or omitted.

If the option is present in some but not all of the descriptions that request the same attribute (directly, through a supertype or through the asterisk), the result is implementation defined.
sections.plainLanguage: When you ask for things, a few must always come in code form, and the rest come the way you asked. If you ask for the same thing two different ways, the server decides what to do.

sections.title: Security and Registration
sections.content:
When interpreting security-sensitive fields, especially those used to grant or deny access, implementations MUST make sure that matching rule comparisons are done on the underlying abstract value, regardless of the encoding used.

For IANA, the binary option is registered in the LDAP attribute description option registry, with Family of Options set to NO and the IESG as change controller.
sections.plainLanguage: Whichever way a value is packed, the server must compare what is inside, not the wrapping, especially when deciding who gets in.
